### 1.1 Methodology and General Themes 

The consumption data in this chapter has been derived using a straightforward apparent consumption methodology.  Therefore for every country and region consumption is: - 

Production of copper wirerod 

_<u>Minus</u>_ exports of copper wirerod and drawn wire _<u>Plus</u>_ imports of copper wirerod and drawn wire _<u>Minus</u>_ stock changes in wirerod and drawn wire 

_<u>Equals</u>_ apparent consumption of copper wirerod and drawn wire

We do, of course, accept that there are stocks of copper wirerod and drawn wire at all stages of the process – at wirerod producers, traders, across the supply chain, and through to wire drawers, and insulated wire and cable manufacturers, as well as at other processors.  The ebb and flow of these stock changes in response to market conditions, logistical considerations and copper prices, creates the feedback pulse that triggers the restocking / destocking cycle that operates in each regional market.  These do much to explain the year-to-year variations (good year - bad year - good year) that is sometimes seen, an

d also sometimes the variations from one quarter to the next within the course of a year. 

The main problem is lack of visibility.  There is some published data on wirerod stock levels at producers for a few national markets, but no data at all on wirerod inventory levels at traders or consumers.  Equally there are no statistics on drawn wire stocks at producers, traders or consumers.  We have therefore decided, in the interests of comparability across all countries and regions, to only identify significant stock changes where they materially affect or distort consumption for one year, or a period of years, for particular countries.  The major problem we have identified concerns Russian wirerod stocks at traders and / or mills.  This aspect is discussed in **Chapter 3 Production and Industry Trends** (pp72-73). 

So by implication, our production, trade and consumption data includes elements of the restocking cycle that amplifies apparent growth (such as was the case in the 8.6% apparent rise in 2004), but equally, also the destocking cycle that dampened apparent growth to 1.3% in 2005. In 2008, despite its weaker fundamental drivers from the cable industry and the world economy, it is clear that destocking is again playing a role, aided by the recent decline in copper prices. 

It is essential to re-emphasise that the copper wirerod market represents a “ _derived demand_ ” for copper rod and drawn wire from the wire and cable industry.  The growth and direction of the world wire and cable industry, in its constituent regional markets, therefore dictates the rate of growth, or decline, that the wirerod industry will see from one year to the next.  Fluctuations in stock levels all the way through the supply chain, from cathode at rod mills to finished wire and cable inventories at consumers, do play a role but the wirerod industry itself has little leverage over the outcome.  Individual rod mills or groups do have a little more influence over their own destinies, but they still have to battle the same tides and currents as the rest of the industry. 

The structure and evolution of the wire and cable market is important for the rod industry on several levels.  At the most basic level it is logical to match the quality of rod to the quality of the type of wire and cable that is being manufactured for the particular end use market that it is intended to serve.  As a general guide, the higher the specification of the wire or cable, and the greater the degree of value added, the more of a necessity it will be to use rod from premium grade cathode as a raw material (e.g. extra high voltage utility power cable).  The other main criterion is how fine the wire needs to be drawn.  The finer the wire, the more essential it is to use premium grade rod to prevent wire breaks (e.g. ultra fine magnet wire, automotive wire or electronic wire). The other main considerations concern wire and cable specifications and whether the customer is a distributor/wholesaler, utility or OEM.  Fixed national standards, regular delivery schedules, multiple delivery locations and a low labour cost component of the total manufacturing cost make it difficult (although not necessarily impossible) for wires and cables to be manufactured a great distance away from where they will be consumed.  This is important because it limits the degree of offshoring or outsourcing that the wire and cable industry can undertake, and limits the threat of international wire and cable imports on distant regional markets.  For example, the requirement for distributors to receive next day delivery of multiple types of building wires made to national US specifications precludes a Chinese manufacturer from serving the US market without establishing a huge logistical supply chain of shipping, warehousing and distribution for this low margin product.  By the same token, the fact that building wire manufacture is a capital intensive process with a very low labour cost component also enables local manufacturers to remain competitive against distant low cost competition.  Equally the need for utilities to receive deliveries of cables to their approved standards to multiple supply depots also precludes supply from a distant location without establishing the same supply chain. All these factors ensure that there is a limit to offshoring or outsourcing certain parts of the wire and cable industry, and that therefore regional rod markets will be preserved to some extent. 

Unfortunately, the same is much less true of the OEM wire and cable sector.  Here “cost is king” and manufacturers of components, assemblies and appliances are flexible and footloose. These companies have constructed global supply chains utilising multiple low cost manufacturing and assembly plants to bring down costs to the lowest possible level.  The autom

otive wiring harness business is probably one of the best examples of this.  Today nearly all wiring harnesses are assembled in Mexico, Central America, Developing Asia, North Africa and Eastern and Central Europe, even though the final automobile is assembled in the US, Germany or Japan.  As wiring harness assembly is labour intensive, it has progressively moved to very low labour cost locations from which finished harnesses or harness sub-assemblies are then shipped or trucked to automobile assembly plants.  The problem for the wire and cable

industry is that once wiring harness assembly moves to say China from Mexico, the Mexican automotive wire producer will lose his contract (as he cannot profitably export to China) and that a Chinese automotive wire producer will win the new contract.  But this doesn’t help the Mexican copper rod producer who in turn loses his contract to supply the Mexican automotive wire producer. 

A similar fate has befallen the US magnet (winding) wire industry since 2000.  The offshore movement of appliance manufacture and automotive components compelled the electric motor industry to follow.  As a result US magnet wire production collapsed, and much of what remained in North America was moved to Mexico to be closer to the electric motor industry that had relocated there.  US magnet wire producers Rea Magnet Wire and Superior Essex now own and run several Chinese magnet wire plants and joint ventures to support the US electric motor manufacturers who have transplant operations there.  But that is no consolation to the US rod industry that no longer supplies them.  Chinese, Taiwanese and South Korean rod mills now supply these US transplant magnet wire plants. 

So depending on the wire and cable production mix, it is possible to gauge the extent to which rod sales in a national market may be vulnerable to future outsourcing or offshoring.  It is inevitable that certain elements and sectors of the wire and cable industry will continue with this process and exploit the potential cost savings that globalisation offers.  For example, the onset of the 2001 recession forced US manufacturers to cut costs, leading to customer migration to lower labour cost locations within (Mexico, Central America) and outside the region (China, Philippines). 

We are already seeing a similar response to the “subprime / credit crunch” slowdown in 2007/2008, so it should not come as a surprise if there is another surge in customer migration, with implications for the wire and cable industry, and then in turn for the wirerod mills that supply them.  This is just as apparent in a European context with the closure wire and cable manufacturing in the higher cost western locations (Ireland, United Kingdom, and France) and expansions in Southern Europe, North Africa and Eastern and Central Europe.  These trends are inevitable and

they are not going to reverse.  The progressive deindustrialisation of the UK wire and cable industry greatly contributed to the decision to close the last remaining rod mill, Prysmian at Prescot.  As the local cable industry closes or relocates and the remaining customers become ever more distant, so rod output falls and closure become inevitable. 

But one company’s closure, offshoring, our outsourcing is another’s opportunity.  The development of the North African wire and cable industry has contributed to the growth of rod production (and La Farga’s new mill) in Spain for export, and has also been the catalyst for the rapid growth in rod production in Egypt.  In the same way, the rapid growth in cable production in the Middle East has presented opportunities for the establishment of a sizeable rod industry to support their growth.  The same is true of India, ASEAN and especially China. 

Substitution, such as the ongoing replacement of copper telecom cables or local area network cables by the superior capability offered by fibre optic cables or wireless technology, is another serious challenge to wire and cable production (and therefore wirerod consumption).  The same applies to other cable uses, such as the decision of a consumer to choose cheaper aluminium windings over more expensive copper windings or less costly aluminium power cables over

copper power cables.  These customer decisions are affecting rod mill margins as some volume has been taken away from copper cable production, which has in turn meant lower copper rod consumption.  Some substitution is inevitable – it always has been with us, and it will be part of the future.  It has been an important consideration recently, but it has not been a critical one.  If the peak in copper prices is indeed now past, and if copper prices continue to trend lower, then it may be that major losses do not materialise.  If copper prices do stay at high levels for a prolonged period of time then substitution losses in copper wire and cable markets could increase, with a consequent reduction in rod volumes. 

This is a concern because up until 2008, the potential to switch from wires and cables with copper conductors to wires and cables with aluminium conductors was limited by capacity constraints in aluminium wirerod supply.  These are now being overcome by new aluminium wirerod projects in Iceland, the Gulf States, India and China, so there is now greater potential for substitution to occur if the price differential is maintained and consumers are persuaded by the benefits. The wire and cable industry has changed from a “neutral” stance on conductor choice to a more “proactive” stance pointing out the cost savings that can be realised by switching to aluminium, optical fibre, copper clad aluminium or copper clad steel alternatives. 

These options may become more attractiv

e as a driver to cut costs in the teeth of a recession. But other factors can also trigger substitution in areas beyond copper’s control. The spiralling price of oil has stimulated research and development spending to develop lightweight copper clad aluminium harness subassemblies for automobiles, and the first models will be appearing in 2010. In quantitative terms the biggest threat would come from a modification in Chinese wire and cable standards and specifications which would favour aluminium or copper clad variants over copper. This would permanently impair future growth prospects for copper wirerod. However neither aluminium, fibre optic, copper clad or wireless technologies can ever hope to displace more than a small proportion of copper wire and cable market. Copper is the premier material on a lifetime cost basis for many end use applications. Moreover, there is insufficient capacity for the substitute materials for wholesale replacement of elements of the copper market over the forecast period of this report. Moreover, at the same time that substitution may be taking volumes away from the market, additional volumes are being created in new applications and by rising intensity of use in existing applications. Renewable energy sources, hybrid vehicles, energy efficiency legislation and the upsizing of wiring gauges are just four of the areas where copper is gaining new markets and additional volumes on a daily basis. Arguably copper has more to benefit from new market and application creation than it has to fear from substitution. If copper supply is rationed in the future by mine and SXEW output constraints, then copper demand will be substituted or economised in heat transfer, malleable or decorative applications where its properties are desirable, but where other materials possess superior characteristics on a lifetime cost basis. Wirerod production tends to follow the trend in wire and cable consumption. Therefore, the best prospects for wirerod consumption are those countries where copper wire and cable production is increasing quickly (due to a combination of inward migration and domestic consumption growth and rising export sales) but where imports of wire and cable are low or declining. However, the reversal of any or all of these factors and the outlook for copper wirerod consumption would deteriorate rapidly. ### 1.2 Main Findings 

- **The world market for copper wirerod and drawn wire rose from 11.3m tonnes in 2000 to 14.3m tonnes in 2007 - a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 3.4%.** 

- **2004 (+8.6%) and 2007 (+5.8%) were the peak years for growth.  2004 was marked by an exceptional synchronised expansion in every region of the world.** 

- **By contrast, 2001 (-0.6%), 2002 (+1.7%) and 2005 (+1.3%) were characterised by below average growth, indicating year-to-year variations and unpredictability.** 

- **The twin forces of economic development and rising electricity consumption have driven global copper wire and cable consumption (and hence production) growth, which ultimately generates demand for copper wirerod and drawn wire.** 

- **But the associated forces of globalisation have sharply polarised where cable production growth has occurred and also, importantly, where it has declined.** 

- **Wirerod and drawn wire demand in Developing Asia, Eastern & Central Europe and the Rest of the World grew at a CAGR of +10% between 2000-2007.** 

- **Meanwhile, wirerod and drawn wire demand in all of North, South and Central America, Western Europe and North East Asia declined at a CAGR of -1%.** 

- **So not only is copper wire and cable production rising faster in emerging markets than in industrialised markets – it is now actually growing at the expense of them.** 

- **The combined share of demand in Developing Asia, Eastern & Central Europe and the Rest of the World exceeded 51% of world consumption in 2007.  This compares to only 33% in 2000 and shows how dramatic the revolution has been.** 

- **North America’s share of world consumption has slumped from 25% to only 15%; Western Europe’s has dipped from 21% to 17%; North East Asia has shrunk from 16% to 13% and South & Central America has fallen from 4% to 3%.** 

- **North American consumption has been in freefall, falling in six of the last seven years.  Almost 25% of the 2.8m tonne market had gone by 2007 (2.2m tonnes). Declines in regional cable production, cable exports and the offshore migration of OEM consumers were the main drivers.  Rising cable imports worsened the blow.** 

- **Consumption in South & Central America only increased by a slow rate of 1.8% per annum from 436kt to 493kt.  Excluding the smaller but faster growing Central American market, demand only grew by 1.3% per annum in South America. Rising cable imports from overseas have blunted local cable industry growth.** 

- **Western European offtake growth has been anaemic, expanding by just 0.7% from 2.35m to 2.49m tonnes over the period.  It was only in 2006 and 2007 that the cable industry has expanded its production beyond the peak achieved in 2000.**

- **Why has the cable industry underperformed?  Cable plant closures in the UK and Ireland; new cablemaking investment has been targeted in Eastern & Central Europe and North Africa; Western Europe has changed from being a modest net exporter of finished wire and cable to modest importer over the 2000-2007 period. Consumers have migrated to Eastern & Central Europe, North Africa and Asia.** 

- **Eastern & Central Europe has witnessed spectacular growth, with consumption doubling from 0.6m tonnes to 1.2m tonnes over the 2000-2007.  This equates to a CAGR of 9.8%.  Growth was even faster in 2007 at an impressive 17.1%.** 

- **The region has benefited from economic development, EU membership, consumer migration from Western Europe, domestic and foreign investment in cablemaking capacity across the region (and progressively further South and East).  The region has increased its net exports of cables to Western Europe and the Middle East.** 

- **The Rest of the World (mainly Africa and the Middle East) has been witness to considerable growth. Copper wirerod and drawn wire demand doubled from 0.6m tonnes in 2000 to 1.2m tonnes by 2007 at a CAGR of 10.1%.  Recent growth was faster at 15.2% in 2007. The expansion was even quicker if Australasia is excluded.** 

- **Economic development, oil wealth, construction and infrastructure projects and tourism have begun to transform parts of these countries.  North Africa has also benefited as an attractive low cost assembly area for Western Europe.  The economic climate has encouraged existing wire and cable plants to expand severalfold, and for many new cablemaking projects to be planned and established.** 

- **North East Asia (Japan, Korea, and Taiwan) has seen its demand for copper wirerod and drawn wire fall at a CAGR of -0.4% from 1.9m to 1.8 million tonnes.** 

- **Despite economic growth, North East Asian consumers have migrated offshore to China, ASEAN and the Indian Subcontinent.  The cable industry has followed to these lower cost manufacturing centres and they have then begun re-exporting back to consumers in North East Asia, further undermining local cable manufacture.** 

- **Developing Asia has been the undisputed winner from the favourable combination of economic development, rising electricity usage, inward consumer migration, sustained rapid investment in cablemaking capacity by locally-owned and overseas companies and a large and growing trade surplus in insulated wires and cables.** 

- **Consumption of copper wirerod and drawn wire has all but doubled from 2.6m tonnes in 2000 to 5.0m tonnes in 2007 at a CAGR of 9.8%.  The rate of expansion was even faster in 2007 with a startling 13.2% increase being achieved.**

The growth in Chinese copper wirerod and drawn wire consumption would have been even faster over the 2000-2007 period but for several factors related to the impact of high copper prices, and the lower absolute and relative price of substitutes. CRU International Limited confidential 1-42 Copper Semis Service – Copper Wirerod Consumption & Market Trends The **Middle East** has registered impressive growth over the 2000-2007 timeframe. Consumption of copper wirerod and drawn wire has almost doubled from 359kt in 2000 to 702kt last year, equivalent to a compound annual growth rate of 10%. 2001 and 2003 were the only years during the period to see negligible increases, of just 0.7% and 3.2%, respectively. However, in all other years the rate of growth has been close to 10%, with the exception of the stellar year of 2007 which saw a 25% surge from 563kt to 702kt. Indeed, 2007 was so exceptional that it accounted for 140kt, or 40%, of all the growth for the region during the whole period. The rise in oil prices since 2000, and their rapid escalation since 2005, has created a massive inflow of wealth into the Middle East. This has fuelled a massive construction and utility infrastructure boom which has in turn created an unprecedented increase in wire and cable

demand. Up until 2006, this increase in regional cable consumption was met by a fairly even combination of an expansion of local cable production and an increase in imports of insulated wire and cable from overseas. In 2007, the boom in demand reached unprecedented proportions. However, because of the expansions in wire and cable capacity within the region, local cablemakers were for the first time in a position to secure the vast majority of the increase in orders that were placed, at the expense of wire and cable imports from overseas. This generated the 40% increase in wirerod and drawn wire consumption in 2007. We have confirmed the magnitude of the expansion across the region during numerous visits from CRU’s wire and cable team to cablemakers within the region over the past twelve months. Saudi Arabia is the leading consumer accounting for 279kt (+50% yoy) of regional offtake, or 40% of the total. Iran is the next largest, with demand of 187kt in 2007 equivalent to a 27% share. The United Arab Emirates was the third ranked user with 80kt in 2007, or an 11% share. Oman is fourth with 61kt equating to a 9% share. Smaller – though still significant copper cable producers – include Kuwait and Israel (both 26kt in 2007), Syria (19kt) and Jordan (16kt). Tiny consumers include the Lebanon, Cyprus, Qatar, Yemen, Malta, Iraq and Bahrain. #### 1.3.13 Africa The African continent has achieved one of the fastest growth rates since 2000. Consumption of copper wirerod and drawn wire has more than doubled from 153kt in 2000, to 349kt in 2007, showing a CAGR of 12.5%. Growth was strongest at the start of the decade, growing by 31% in 2001. Demand was a more moderate 13-14% in 2002 and 2003. In 2004, growth stagnated as higher copper prices restrained affordability. In 2005, wire and cable production in the region recovered and wirerod consumption with it, when growth topped 16%. The industry grew at more moderate single digit rates in 2006 and 2007. There are several reasons for the strong expansion of African wirerod demand. Firstly, there has been a migration to Africa from some higher cost production centres, mostly in Southern Europe. Secondly, some economies in Africa have seen a strong improvement themselves; these are particularly countries in North and Southern Africa. Consequently, wirerod consumption and wire and cable production has increased to serve both increasing domestic demand and rising exports. Libya and Nigeria have also benefited from being oil producers.
